key_concepts.name: Defensive Stance and Ready Position
key_concepts.summary: A basketball defensive stance is a loaded, mobile position rather than a static squat: feet outside hip width, knees and hips flexed, chest balanced over the base, active hands, eyes scanning ball and body cues, and weight ready to push, slide, turn, sprint, or jump. It supports on-ball containment, denial, help, closeout braking, box-out contact, and repeated efforts.
coaching_cues: Low enough to move, not so low that the first step is slow.
Chest over hips, hips over feet.
Hands work without reaching across the offensive player's body.
Move from stance into sprint, turn, slide, or jump without standing up first.

common_errors.error: Deep static squat with feet too wide.
common_errors.correction: Use short reactive bursts from a stance that allows push-off, hip turn, and recovery sprint.

common_errors.error: Hands down while guarding live ball.
common_errors.correction: Teach one hand influencing the ball and one hand ready to contest, stunt, or trace without fouling.

common_errors.error: Standing upright during off-ball defense.
common_errors.correction: Use open stance and pistol stance checks in shell drill so players see ball and matchup.

progression.beginner: Learn stance, balance, legal space, hand activity, and basic slide-run recovery over short distances.
progression.intermediate: Add closeout into containment, denial stance, help stance, and recover-to-box-out sequences.
progression.advanced: Blend stance with tactical footwork: angle force, switch, peel, stunt, tag roller, rebound, and sprint in transition.

source_refs: Courses Available Through the E-Learning Program

key_concepts.name: Closeout: Fast-Slow, Angle, Contest, Contain
key_concepts.summary: Closeouts connect team defense to individual containment. The defender covers ground while the ball travels, brakes with short choppy steps, arrives on an angle that removes the highest-value shot or drive, contests without leaving their feet unnecessarily, and then guards the first dribble.
coaching_cues: Sprint while the pass is in the air.
Brake early enough to absorb the first drive.
High hand to shooting pocket; hips angled to the scouting force.
Contest, land balanced, then guard the next action.

common_errors.error: Flying past the shooter.
common_errors.correction: Use a fast-slow closeout with earlier deceleration and a lower last two steps.

common_errors.error: Stopping short and allowing rhythm catch-and-shoot threes.
common_errors.correction: Measure closeout distance by shooter range and release speed, not a fixed spot.

common_errors.error: Jumping on every shot fake.
common_errors.correction: Teach hand contest with feet down unless the scout requires a full vertical contest.

progression.beginner: Partner pass-closeout-contain with no shot fake.
progression.intermediate: Add shot fake, one-dribble drive, and closeout-to-box-out.
progression.advanced: Use advantage closeouts from rotations, late-clock fly-bys, no-middle/no-baseline rules, and scout-based closeout speeds.

source_refs: Courses Available Through the E-Learning Program

key_concepts.name: On-Ball Containment and Force Rules
key_concepts.summary: Containment means keeping the ball in front long enough for the defense to stay organized. The force rule determines where the ball is allowed to go: sideline, weak hand, away from a screen, toward help, or away from the middle. Good containment combines footwork, angle, chest discipline, legal contact, and awareness of help location.
coaching_cues: Influence the ball, do not open both gates.
Slide when you can, turn-and-run when you must, recover chest-first.
Do not reach from behind after being beaten.
Know the help before choosing pressure level.

common_errors.error: Trying to steal instead of contain.
common_errors.correction: Grade possessions on paint touches denied and body position, not only steals.

common_errors.error: Forcing baseline when no baseline help is loaded.
common_errors.correction: Make the force rule explicit before live play and rehearse help-side spots.

progression.beginner: Guard a dribbler in lanes with no screen and one clear force direction.
progression.intermediate: Add live 1v1 from wing, slot, and corner with help-side reference cones.
progression.advanced: Add scout-based weak-hand force, late-clock pressure, switch containment, and foul-avoidance in bonus situations.

key_concepts.name: Help Defense and Shell Positioning
key_concepts.summary: Shell defense teaches five players to guard the ball, their own matchup, and the basket at the same time. Off-ball defenders adjust by ball location: one pass away may deny, gap, or stunt; two passes away should usually load to help, see ball and player, protect the paint, and be ready to rotate or rebound.
coaching_cues: Ball-you-man vision unless denying by plan.
Move on the pass, not after the catch.
Help early enough to stop the drive, recover early enough to contest the next shot.
Every rotation ends with a matchup and a box-out.

common_errors.error: Watching only the ball and losing cutters.
common_errors.correction: Use pistol stance checks and cutter-call accountability in shell.

common_errors.error: Helping from the strong-side corner without a clear rotation.
common_errors.correction: Define no-help spots and low-man responsibilities.

common_errors.error: Rotating but failing to rebound.
common_errors.correction: Finish every shell possession with a shot and assigned box-outs.

progression.beginner: 2v2 and 3v3 shell: ball, deny/gap, help, recover.
progression.intermediate: 4v4 shell with drive-and-kick, cutters, baseline drive, and skip pass.
progression.advanced: 5v5 shell with random screens, pick-and-roll tags, X-outs, scram switches, and late-clock rotations.

key_concepts.name: Rotations, Low Man, X-Outs, and Next Defense
key_concepts.summary: Modern basketball defense often requires a temporary two-on-one sacrifice to stop the ball or roller, followed by a chain rotation. The low man protects the rim or tags the roller; the next defender covers the first pass; X-outs solve corner-wing closeouts; and the final defender must find the most dangerous remaining player.
coaching_cues: Stop the ball first, then solve the matchup.
Low man tags with body presence, then recovers on the pass.
Next defender takes the nearest most dangerous threat.
Communicate the rotation before contact, not after the pass is made.

common_errors.error: Two defenders recover to the same shooter.
common_errors.correction: Install 'next' language and require the second rotator to call the open player.

common_errors.error: Late low-man tag gives up a direct roll layup.
common_errors.correction: Start the tag as the screener rolls, not after the catch.

progression.intermediate: 4v4 baseline drive and corner lift rotations.
progression.advanced: 5v5 pick-and-roll tags, X-outs, peel switches, and scram switches against mismatch hunting.

key_concepts.name: Pick-and-Roll Coverage Family
key_concepts.summary: Pick-and-roll defense is a coverage family, not one technique. Common coverages include over, under, drop, hedge/show-and-recover, switch, ice/fan, blitz/trap, late switch, veer-back, and peel. The correct choice depends on ball-handler shooting, screener rolling/pop threat, spacing, clock, foul context, and personnel.
coaching_cues: Call the coverage early and loudly.
On-ball defender owns screen navigation; screener defender owns ball delay and roller recovery.
Weak-side defenders must tag, bump, and rotate by coverage.
Coverage success is judged by shot quality, foul count, and rebound, not only whether the ball handler scores.

common_errors.error: The on-ball defender dies on the screen.
common_errors.correction: Teach screen alerts, body angle, shoulder-through technique, and urgent rear-view pursuit.

common_errors.error: Big defender shows high but no one tags the roller.
common_errors.correction: Pair every hedge/show coverage with low-man tag and weak-side rotation rules.

common_errors.error: Switching without addressing size mismatch.
common_errors.correction: Install switch-back, scram, front/post help, or immediate double rules.

progression.beginner: 2v2 ball-screen introduction: call screen, get over/under, recover.
progression.intermediate: 3v3 with corner tagger: drop, hedge, switch, ice, and roller reads.
progression.advanced: 5v5 scout-based coverages with ghost screens, slips, short rolls, empty-side pick-and-roll, Spain action, and late-clock automatic switches.

key_concepts.name: Screen Navigation: On-Ball and Off-Ball
key_concepts.summary: Screen navigation requires early communication, body contact without holding, correct path selection, and recovery angle. Defenders may chase, trail, lock-and-trail, go under, shoot the gap, top-lock, switch, bump, peel, or deny the screen depending on shooter threat and team coverage.
coaching_cues: See the screen early or hear it early.
Get skinny through legal space; do not grab or displace.
Trail shooters tight; go under non-shooters only by plan.
After navigating, square the ball and rebound.

common_errors.error: No verbal screen call.
common_errors.correction: Make the screener defender call direction and coverage before screen contact.

common_errors.error: Chasing every shooter the same way.
common_errors.correction: Teach scout categories: elite shooter, driver, screener, non-shooter, and slip threat.

common_errors.error: Illegal holding through off-ball screens.
common_errors.correction: Use footwork and shoulder angle instead of arms to maintain position.

progression.beginner: Stationary down-screen and flare-screen reads at walk-through speed.
progression.intermediate: Live 2v2 off-ball screening with chase, under, and switch calls.
progression.advanced: Stagger, pin-down, flare, hammer, Spain, and screening-the-screener sequences with multiple coverages.

source_refs: Courses Available Through the E-Learning Program

key_concepts.name: Transition Defense Priorities
key_concepts.summary: Transition defense begins before possession changes. Teams must balance offensive rebounding with floor balance, sprint back, stop the ball, protect the basket, match up from inside out, communicate cross-matches, and only then locate original assignments. Shot selection, turnover location, and crash rules heavily influence transition exposure.
coaching_cues: First three steps are a sprint.
Ball, basket, then shooters.
Build a wall early; do not retreat under the rim.
Talk cross-match, then clean up matchups when the ball is contained.

common_errors.error: Everyone watches the shot or turnover.
common_errors.correction: Assign crash, safety, and sprint-back roles by lineup and shot location.

common_errors.error: Stopping at the paint while the ball handler attacks downhill.
common_errors.correction: Meet the ball above the scoring area with help behind.

common_errors.error: Running to own player instead of stopping immediate danger.
common_errors.correction: Use cross-match rules: nearest stops ball, next protects rim, next finds shooter.

progression.intermediate: 4v3 and 5v4 conversion from missed shots, turnovers, and live rebounds.
progression.advanced: Scout-based transition defense with crash-safety tradeoffs, drag screens, early seals, corner fills, and take-foul rule awareness.

source_refs: Courses Available Through the E-Learning Program

key_concepts.name: Defensive Rebounding: Finish the Stop
key_concepts.summary: A defensive stop is incomplete until the ball is secured. Defensive rebounding combines shot recognition, contact, displacement prevention, pursuit, high-point catch, chin/protect, outlet decision, and transition awareness. Guards and perimeter defenders must rebound because long shots create long rebounds and teams increasingly space four or five players.
coaching_cues: Hit first, find, pursue, secure.
Interior box-outs may require back contact; perimeter box-outs need vision and containment.
Rebound outside your area.
Outlet only after possession is controlled.

common_errors.error: Watching the flight of the shot before making contact.
common_errors.correction: Train shot-call, contact-check, then pursue sequence.

common_errors.error: Turning back on a perimeter crash and giving up a run-in rebound.
common_errors.correction: Use T-up or shoulder-chest contact for perimeter box-outs while keeping vision.

common_errors.error: Tipping rebounds blindly in traffic.
common_errors.correction: Teach two-hand high-point catches and strong chin/pivot under pressure.

progression.intermediate: Square rebounding with rotating assignments and live outlet.
progression.advanced: 5v5 rebound-to-transition with crash scouts, switch mismatches, long-rebound zones, and late-game free-throw blockouts.

source_refs: Advanced Rebounding: Secrets From The Pros

key_concepts.name: Offensive Rebounding and Conversion Balance
key_concepts.summary: Offensive rebounding can create high-value second chances but increases transition-defense risk if crash roles are poorly defined. Teams should decide who crashes, who sprints back, and who temporarily jams outlet lanes based on shot location, lineup, score, time, and opponent transition threat.
coaching_cues: Crash from advantage spots, not from every spot.
One or two designated safeties must be visible as the shot goes up.
If you cannot rebound, delay the outlet or sprint back.
After an offensive rebound, reset spacing before forcing a bad putback.

common_errors.error: All five crash and concede uncontested transition layups.
common_errors.correction: Install crash-safety rules by position, shot location, and game context.

common_errors.error: No one crashes from the weak side.
common_errors.correction: Teach weak-side anticipation because many misses rebound opposite the shot side.

progression.beginner: Teach shot-follow, weak-side crash, and safety spots in controlled 3v3.
progression.intermediate: 4v4/5v5 with crash points and immediate conversion scoring.
progression.advanced: Opponent-specific crash plan: punish small lineups, avoid elite transition teams, attack late-clock long rebounds.

source_refs: 5 Simple Ways to Improve Your Basketball Rebounding

key_concepts.name: Defensive Communication System
key_concepts.summary: Communication turns five individual defenders into a unit. Useful calls include ball, help, deny, gap, screen left/right, under, over, switch, ice, drop, show, tag, low, next, box, shot, cutter, dead, foul, no three, and timeout/foul-clock reminders. Calls must be early, short, actionable, and tied to team vocabulary.
coaching_cues: Early, loud, repeated.
Call coverage plus direction, not just 'screen'.
Back-line defenders see more and must lead rotations.
Echo calls so the whole team hears the same coverage.

common_errors.error: Talking after the action has already beaten the defense.
common_errors.correction: Score practices for early calls and require coverage calls before screen contact.

common_errors.error: Too many words in live play.
common_errors.correction: Use one-word or two-word calls with pre-taught meanings.

progression.beginner: Require ball/help/shot/box calls in shell and rebounding.
progression.intermediate: Add screen-direction, coverage, cutter, and low-man calls.
progression.advanced: Add scout, clock, foul, switch/scram, special-situation, and no-timeout communication.

source_refs: Courses Available Through the E-Learning Program

key_concepts.name: Matchup, Zone, and Hybrid Defense Principles
key_concepts.summary: Man-to-man, matchup zone, 2-3, 3-2, 1-3-1, box-and-one, triangle-and-two, and switching defenses all require ball pressure, paint protection, rebounding assignments, and communication. Zone defense reduces some matchup problems but can concede offensive rebounds and corner/skips if rotations and block-outs are vague.
coaching_cues: Guard areas, then match bodies on shots.
Do not let zone become standing.
Pressure the ball enough to slow passing rhythm.
Every zone possession still needs shot, hit, and pursue.

common_errors.error: Zone defenders point instead of moving.
common_errors.correction: Teach zone slides, bump rules, closeout assignments, and rebounding matchups.

common_errors.error: Box-and-one leaves non-target players unguarded on cuts and rebounds.
common_errors.correction: Define who protects the rim, who covers short corner, and who blocks out each zone.

progression.beginner: Introduce man-to-man shell before zone so players learn responsibility and ball-player vision.
progression.intermediate: Teach 2-3 or 3-2 rotations with clear corner, high-post, short-corner, and rebounding rules.
progression.advanced: Use matchup zone, junk defenses, switching zones, late-clock zone, and after-timeout disguise packages.

source_refs: Investigating the Effect of Playing Different Defensive Styles and Court Sizes on Physical, Perceived, and Technical Demands in Basketball Small-Sided Games

key_concepts.name: Post Defense and Paint Protection
key_concepts.summary: Post defense starts before the catch. Options include full front, three-quarter front, behind, push-out, dig, stunt, double, and baseline trap. The team must decide where help comes from and how to rotate out because overhelping from shooters or late digs can produce high-value kick-out threes.
coaching_cues: Work early to move the catch away from the rim.
Chest and leverage before hands.
Dig on the dribble, recover on the pickup.
Low man protects the rim without abandoning the next most dangerous shooter.

common_errors.error: Defender lets the post catch two feet from the rim, then fights late.
common_errors.correction: Teach early contact, three-quarter positioning, and push-out before the pass.

common_errors.error: Double team comes from the wrong shooter.
common_errors.correction: Pre-call double source based on spacing and scouting report.

progression.beginner: 1v1 post position without fouling and basic rebound.
progression.intermediate: 2v2/3v3 post feed, dig, and kick-out recoveries.
progression.advanced: 5v5 fronting, weak-side lob help, baseline trap, late-clock dig, and mismatch post-scram.

key_concepts.name: End-Game and Special Situations Defense
key_concepts.summary: Late-game defense changes with score, time, fouls, timeouts, possession arrow/rules context, and opponent personnel. Teams need explicit rules for no-three, foul-up-three, no-foul, intentional foul timing, switch-everything, defend-without-fouling in the bonus, sideline/baseline out-of-bounds, free-throw rebounding, jump-ball/held-ball, and last-shot rebounding.
coaching_cues: Know score, time, fouls, timeout status, and shooter locations.
No-three means top-side shooters, switch or foul before the shot only if legal and planned.
No-foul means chest containment, vertical contests, and no reach from behind.
On final shot, rebound until the horn.

common_errors.error: Players do not know whether to foul or defend.
common_errors.correction: Practice score-time-foul scripts and require point guard/back-line reminders.

common_errors.error: Switch-everything creates an immediate post mismatch with no plan.
common_errors.correction: Use switch-plus-scram or switch-and-front rules.

common_errors.error: Celebrating a missed shot before securing the rebound.
common_errors.correction: Rehearse final-possession rebounding, tip control, and timeout/outlet decisions.

progression.beginner: Teach score-time awareness and no-foul defense in simple 3v3.
progression.intermediate: Add sideline/baseline out-of-bounds and free-throw rebounding scenarios.
progression.advanced: Simulate late-game packages: down one, up three, in bonus, no timeout, foul-to-give, switch all, deny star, and rebound-to-timeout.

technical_models.name: Stance-to-Movement Chain
sequence: Recognize ball status and offensive threat.
Load into balanced stance with active hands and vision.
Choose movement: slide, crossover run, hip turn, backpedal, jump, stunt, or closeout.
Reestablish legal guarding position or help position.
Finish with contest, rebound, recovery, or transition sprint.
technical_models.coaching_application: Use to prevent isolated stance drills from becoming non-transferable. Every stance rep should connect to a basketball decision and next effort.
source_refs: High-Intensity Acceleration and Deceleration Demands in Elite Team Sports Competitive Match Play: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

technical_models.name: Closeout Decision Tree
decision_points: Is the receiver an elite shooter, average shooter, driver, or non-shooter?
Is the closeout long, medium, or short?
What is the force rule and clock context?
Does the receiver have shot, drive, pass, or post advantage?
outputs: Fly-by only by late-clock or scout instruction

technical_models.name: Shell Help-Recover Model
layers: One-pass-away defender denies, gaps, or stunts by team rule.
Two-pass-away defender protects paint with open/pistol stance.
Low man protects rim and tags roller.
Next rotation covers first pass out.
technical_models.coaching_application: Build from 2v2 shell to 5v5 with cutters, drive-and-kick, screens, and shot/rebound finishes.

coverage_options.best_when: Screener defender protects rim, ball handler is less dangerous as pull-up shooter, and roller is a major rim threat.
coverage_options.risk: Pull-up threes, pocket passes, and downhill floaters.

coverage_options.best_when: Ball handler must be delayed and big can recover; weak-side tag is organized.
coverage_options.risk: Short-roll playmaking and late roller recovery.

coverage_options.best_when: Personnel can guard multiple positions or late clock requires no advantage.
coverage_options.risk: Mismatch hunting, offensive rebounding mismatch, and post seals.

coverage_options.best_when: Side pick-and-roll can be kept away from the middle and help is loaded along the sideline/baseline.
coverage_options.risk: Rejects, rescreens, slips, and weak baseline help failures.

coverage_options.best_when: Elite ball handler must give the ball up or clock/score supports aggression.
coverage_options.risk: Four-on-three short-roll attack and skip passes.

coverage_options.best_when: Ball handler is a low pull-up threat and screen is high or flat.
coverage_options.risk: Rhythm pull-up if the scouting evaluation is wrong.

technical_models.name: Screen Navigation Path Model
paths: Chase or lock-and-trail for dangerous shooters.
Go under against non-shooters or deep screens.
Top-lock to deny a shooter from using a pin-down.
Shoot the gap when there is legal space and the receiver is not an elite shooter.
Switch when matchups, clock, or coverage dictate.
Bump or peel when a defender is screened out and the next defender must momentarily take the cutter.

technical_models.name: Contact-Pursuit-Secure Rebounding Model
phases: Identify nearest offensive threat or assigned zone.
Make legal contact to prevent run-in momentum.
Release and pursue the ball outside immediate area.
High-point with two hands when possible.
Secure, chin, pivot, outlet, or put back based on possession and pressure.
source_refs: 5 Simple Ways to Improve Your Basketball Rebounding
Advanced Rebounding: Secrets From The Pros

technical_models.name: Conversion Defense Model
priority_order: Shot selection and turnover prevention reduce transition exposure.
Crash-safety roles are decided before the shot.
Nearest defender stops the ball above the scoring area.
Next defender protects the basket and takes away rim run.
Next defenders fan out to shooters and communicate cross-matches.
Team reorganizes to normal matchups only after the ball is contained.
source_refs: Courses Available Through the E-Learning Program

technical_models.name: Defensive IQ Scan Model
scan_order: Score, time, fouls, timeout status, possession/rules context.
Most dangerous offensive player and spacing.
Next pass, next rotation, and transition consequence.
source_refs: Courses Available Through the E-Learning Program

tactical_rules.name: Defense Ends With a Rebound
tactical_rules.rule: Treat a forced miss as only half a stop until the defense secures possession or clearly controls the ball.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Every defensive drill should periodically finish with a shot, box-out, rebound, outlet, or conversion.

tactical_rules.name: Move on the Pass
tactical_rules.rule: Defenders should adjust while the ball is in the air so they arrive before the catch rather than reacting after the catch.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Coach with pass-flight cues: jump to ball, load to help, closeout, or rotate as the pass leaves the passer's hands.

tactical_rules.name: Transition: Ball, Basket, Shooters
tactical_rules.rule: In transition defense, first stop the ball, then protect the basket, then fan out to shooters and matchups.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Cross-matching is expected; running to an original assignment is secondary to stopping immediate scoring threats.

tactical_rules.name: Force Rule Must Match Help
tactical_rules.rule: Do not teach no-middle, no-baseline, sideline, or weak-hand force as isolated slogans; the force direction must match the location and timing of help.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: If help is absent, the on-ball defender must prioritize containment over the nominal force direction.

tactical_rules.name: Low Man Owns the First Rim Threat
tactical_rules.rule: Against ball-screen advantage, the low man is responsible for early rim protection or roller tag until the coverage resolves.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: The tag must be early enough to alter the roll but controlled enough to recover or trigger the next rotation.

tactical_rules.name: Switching Requires a Second Plan
tactical_rules.rule: A switch is incomplete unless the team knows how to handle the likely mismatch, rebound matchup, post seal, and next screen.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Pair switching with scram, front, late double, switch-back, or rebound gang rules.

tactical_rules.name: Screen Calls Before Contact
tactical_rules.rule: Screen direction and coverage must be communicated before the screened defender is hit.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Use accountable vocabulary: 'screen left, under', 'screen right, switch', 'pin down, chase', not just 'screen'.

tactical_rules.name: Closeout Includes the Next Action
tactical_rules.rule: A closeout is not complete at the contest; the defender must also contain the drive, navigate a shot fake, switch if called, or box out.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Drills that end at the closeout teach incomplete defense; add one or two live decisions.

tactical_rules.name: Perimeter Box-Outs Need Vision
tactical_rules.rule: Perimeter defenders should often use shoulder-chest or T-up contact rather than fully turning their back, because long rebounds and perimeter crashers require vision and containment.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Interior box-outs and perimeter box-outs are different skills; teach both.

tactical_rules.name: Zone Still Blocks Out
tactical_rules.rule: Zone defenders must locate bodies when the shot goes up; area responsibility does not replace rebounding responsibility.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Assign rebound zones and matchup rules for corner, high-post, short-corner, and weak-side crashers.

tactical_rules.name: Foul Context Changes Defense
tactical_rules.rule: Bonus, foul trouble, late-game strategy, and opponent free-throw skill should alter pressure, reach risk, contest choice, and intentional-foul decisions.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Add score-time-foul constraints to live defensive segments.

tactical_rules.name: Crash-Safety Tradeoff
tactical_rules.rule: Offensive rebounding aggression must be balanced against transition-defense safety based on lineup, shot location, and opponent transition threat.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Define who crashes, who gets back, and who delays the outlet before shots are taken.

tactical_rules.name: No Strong-Corner Help Without a Rotation Plan
tactical_rules.rule: Helping from the strong-side corner often gives up a high-value corner three unless the rotation is pre-planned or the rim threat is immediate.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Make no-help and emergency-help locations explicit in scouting.

tactical_rules.name: Late Clock Reduce Complexity
tactical_rules.rule: As the shot clock or game clock falls, defenses should simplify: switch more, avoid unnecessary help, contest without fouling, and rebound.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Practice late-clock coverage calls separately because normal coverage may be too slow or rotation-heavy.

tactical_rules.name: Scout Changes Technique
tactical_rules.rule: Closeout speed, screen path, pick-and-roll coverage, post help, and rebounding matchups should change based on opponent strengths, not habit.
tactical_rules.teaching_note: Use simple scout labels for players: shooter, driver, roller, popper, cutter, post, non-shooter, crash threat.

physical_demands.name: Repeated Deceleration and Braking
physical_demands.description: Closeouts, transition stops, change-of-direction containment, and late rotations impose high braking demands. Defensive drills must prepare athletes to decelerate from sprinting into low, balanced, decision-ready positions.
physical_demands.coaching_implication: Progress closeout distances, speeds, and decision complexity; avoid jumping directly from controlled footwork to chaotic long closeouts.
source_refs: High-Intensity Acceleration and Deceleration Demands in Elite Team Sports Competitive Match Play: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Physical demands of collegiate basketball practice

physical_demands.name: Lateral and Multidirectional Movement
physical_demands.description: On-ball containment and screen navigation require slides, hip turns, crossover runs, backpedals, stunts, and recovery sprints rather than only classic step-slides.
physical_demands.coaching_implication: Teach slide-run transitions and hip mobility under tactical constraints instead of isolated lane slides only.
source_refs: Physical demands of collegiate basketball practice

physical_demands.name: Jump, Contact, and Rebound Load
physical_demands.description: Rebounding and contests combine vertical jumping, body contact, aerial tracking, landing in traffic, and rapid second jumps.
physical_demands.coaching_implication: Train landing mechanics, two-hand securing, contact tolerance, and rebound decision-making with progressive opponent pressure.
source_refs: Sports Injuries in Basketball Players: A Systematic Review
Biomechanics and situational patterns associated with anterior cruciate ligament injuries in the National Basketball Association

physical_demands.name: Multiple-Effort Defensive Sequences
physical_demands.description: A single possession may require closeout, contain, help, recover, screen navigation, tag, second closeout, contest, box-out, and transition sprint.
physical_demands.coaching_implication: Condition defense through short, intense, decision-rich bouts with adequate recovery and technical quality rather than only long running.
source_refs: Courses Available Through the E-Learning Program
The effects of defensive style and final game outcome on the external training load of professional basketball players

physical_demands.name: Defensive Style Alters Load
physical_demands.description: Pressing, trapping, switching, man-to-man, and zone structures can change acceleration, contact, perceived exertion, and technical action profiles.
physical_demands.coaching_implication: Do not assume all defensive practices have the same load. Track defensive style, court size, possession length, and player role.
source_refs: The effects of defensive style and final game outcome on the external training load of professional basketball players
Investigating the Effect of Playing Different Defensive Styles and Court Sizes on Physical, Perceived, and Technical Demands in Basketball Small-Sided Games

physical_demands.name: Transition Sprint and Recovery Demand
physical_demands.description: Conversion defense and offensive rebounding balance require repeated full-court or half-court sprints after shots, turnovers, and loose balls.
physical_demands.coaching_implication: Train conversion from live basketball events, not only baseline running, so players learn sprint priority and communication under fatigue.
source_refs: Physical demands of collegiate basketball practice

injury_or_load_risks.name: Ankle and Knee Injury Risk During Rebounding
injury_or_load_risks.description: Rebounding involves jumping, landing near other players, body contact, and unpredictable ball flight. Basketball injury literature identifies ankle and knee injuries as common, with rebounding situations a notable mechanism.
mitigations: Progress contact rebounding from controlled to live.
Teach vertical landing, space awareness, and two-foot balance.
Avoid excessive blind tipping and undercutting.
Use workload monitoring for high-volume rebounding sessions.
source_refs: Sports Injuries in Basketball Players: A Systematic Review
Biomechanics and situational patterns associated with anterior cruciate ligament injuries in the National Basketball Association

injury_or_load_risks.name: Closeout Deceleration Overload
injury_or_load_risks.description: Long closeouts and transition stops create high eccentric braking loads, especially when athletes are fatigued or asked to react to shot fakes and drives.
mitigations: Limit early-session volume of long closeout reps.
Build braking strength and technique before chaotic closeouts.
Alternate high-speed closeout drills with teaching/recovery blocks.
Use shorter closeouts for younger or returning athletes.
source_refs: High-Intensity Acceleration and Deceleration Demands in Elite Team Sports Competitive Match Play: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
Physical demands of collegiate basketball practice

injury_or_load_risks.name: Illegal Contact, Displacement, and Foul Risk
injury_or_load_risks.description: Poor defensive technique around screens, post defense, charges, box-outs, and closeouts increases foul risk and player safety risk.
mitigations: Teach legal guarding position, cylinder, and verticality.
Use chest and feet rather than grabbing or extending arms.
Practice contesting without landing into the shooter.
Coach box-outs as legal contact and pursuit, not pushing.

injury_or_load_risks.name: Screen Collision Risk
injury_or_load_risks.description: Late screen recognition can produce high-impact collisions, shoulder/neck contact, illegal holds, and defensive players losing balance into other players.
mitigations: Require early screen calls.
Teach legal navigation paths and body angle.
Use controlled screen contact progressions before live screening.
Differentiate blind screens, ball screens, and off-ball screens.
source_refs: Courses Available Through the E-Learning Program

injury_or_load_risks.name: Pressing and Trapping Fatigue
injury_or_load_risks.description: Aggressive full-court pressure and trapping require repeated accelerations, decelerations, reaches, contacts, and recovery sprints, which can degrade technique and increase foul or injury risk.
mitigations: Use short work bouts with clear quality standards.
Track player load and perceived exertion by defensive style.
Rotate personnel and adjust coverage late in games.
Coach vertical chest containment when fatigued.
source_refs: The effects of defensive style and final game outcome on the external training load of professional basketball players
Investigating the Effect of Playing Different Defensive Styles and Court Sizes on Physical, Perceived, and Technical Demands in Basketball Small-Sided Games

injury_or_load_risks.name: Landing After Contest or Shot-Block Attempt
injury_or_load_risks.description: Contests and shot-block attempts can create risky landings when the defender jumps forward, lands on feet, or rotates in the air.
mitigations: Prioritize verticality and high-hand contests.
Discourage unnecessary shot-fake jumps.
Teach land-and-play balance after contests.
Use no-foul contest constraints in practice.
source_refs: Biomechanics and situational patterns associated with anterior cruciate ligament injuries in the National Basketball Association

injury_or_load_risks.name: Youth Tactical Overcomplexity
injury_or_load_risks.description: Young players can be overloaded by advanced zones, traps, and scripted coverages before they understand stance, containment, help, and rebounding fundamentals.
mitigations: Use man-to-man and small-sided games to teach responsibility first.
Add zone or junk defenses only after players can guard ball and player.
Use simple vocabulary and fewer coverage choices for beginners.
Prioritize development over short-term confusion tactics.

training_implications.name: Train Defense as a Possession Chain
training_implications.recommendation: Design drills that link closeout, containment, help, recovery, screen defense, rebound, and transition. Avoid stopping reps after one technical action unless teaching a new skill.
example_progression: 5v5 live conversion after rebound or turnover.

training_implications.name: Use Small-Sided Games for Tactical IQ
training_implications.recommendation: 2v2, 3v3, and 4v4 create more defensive decisions per player than full 5v5 while preserving spacing, help, screen, and rebounding concepts.
example_constraints: Defense scores for three stops in a row.
Offense gets extra point for paint touch; defense must deny paint.
Shot must be rebounded before possession ends.
Coach calls coverage immediately before a ball screen.

training_implications.name: Teach Coverage Vocabulary Early
training_implications.recommendation: Install a small, consistent call system before adding complex coverages. Players cannot execute drop, hedge, ice, switch, or X-out if the words are unclear.

training_implications.name: Finish Defensive Drills With Rebounding
training_implications.recommendation: Most half-court defensive drills should include a shot, box-out, rebound, outlet, or putback consequence so players learn that positioning and rotations are incomplete without possession.
example_constraints: Defense cannot rotate out until it rebounds.
Offense gets two points for offensive rebound.
Defensive rebound starts immediate 3v2 or 5v5 transition.

training_implications.name: Balance Technical and Tactical Load
training_implications.recommendation: Progress from clean technique to live pressure by adding one variable at a time: speed, decision, contact, space, clock, score, fatigue, and scouting.

training_implications.name: Periodize Defensive Intensity
training_implications.recommendation: Pressing, trapping, long closeouts, and live rebounding are high-load blocks. Manage them across the week and season rather than stacking all defensive stressors daily.

training_implications.name: Build Scout-Based Adaptability
training_implications.recommendation: Advanced players should practice changing closeout, screen navigation, coverage, and help decisions based on opponent labels, not just executing one base system.
example_scout_labels: Send extra body to elite offensive rebounder.

training_implications.name: Rehearse End-Game Defense
training_implications.recommendation: Late-game defense should be practiced as a separate skill because score, time, fouls, bonus, and timeout rules change correct decisions.
example_scenarios: Up three, defend without fouling a shooter.
Foul to give with six seconds left.
Need rebound on missed free throw.
Down one, trap without fouling in backcourt.
